newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: World grain ship trade seen over 200 mln T in 2000.
newsitem.headline: World grain ship trade seen over 200 mln T in 2000.

text.p: Total world seaborne trade in grains is forecast to reach 202.3 million tonnes in 2000, from 180.1 million tonnes in 1995, Stephan Hanrahan, director of Ocean Shipping Consultants told a conference here on Thursday.

"The pattern of seaborne trade which will emerge from the overall growth in grain supply and demand forecast...will be increasingly weighted toward the Far East and, to a lesser extent Canada, Australia and Argentina," he said.
In the period between 1995-2000 seaborne wheat imports are projected to increase by 5.0 percent to 88.5 million tonnes and those of coarse grains by 19 percent to 113.8 million tonnes.
Hanrahan said the slower growth anticipated in the wheat trade is largely predicated on the increasing substitution of imports by domestic supplies in China.
Looking farther forward, the U.K.-based consultant, forecast Asia would increase its share of world grain imports from 42.1 percent in 1995 to 48.8 percent in 2010.

The growth in Far East trade will largely be met by North America and Australia as the nearest available suppliers, with Argentina relatively less significant in a projected increase in The Americas share of this market to 18.7 percent in 2010 compared with 15.8 percent in 1995, he said.

"The continued growth in importance of long-haul trades to the Far East will also lead to a continuing slow rise in the average shipping distance. This means that grain shipping demand will increase at a more rapid rate than trade," Hanrahan said.

He said the increasing importance of less developed and newly industrialising markets with less sophisticated port facilities will continue to restrict the deployment of large vessels in the grain trades.
"Thus, grain grain shipping will continue to be dominated by Handy Size and Panamax tonnage, although a marginal increase in the role of Cape size vessels is also anticipated."

Hanrahan said with a projected decline in the EU's share of international grain trade, a forecast increase in demand from North Africa and the Middle East will have to be met largely by North America, particularly the U.S. and Australia.

The regions are within a short or medium haul of possible new sources of supply such as Russia, the Ukraine, other East European countries and India, which would therefore be likely to find markets here as well as in the Far East, he said.
